title: RIP Version 2
subtitle: The small-network routing protocol that learned to carry subnet masks, next hops and a password.
summary: RIP version 2 extends the Routing Information Protocol, a distance-vector protocol in which routers periodically tell their neighbours how far away every network is. Version 2 keeps the same message layout but puts the unused space in each route entry to work, adding a subnet mask, a next hop, a route tag, multicast delivery to 224.0.0.9 and a simple password. It is an Internet Standard (STD 56) and is still used on small networks.

eli5.summary: Every half minute each router tells its neighbours, "here is how many steps I am from every street." Version 2 adds the size of each neighbourhood, a better pointer to the shortest way, and a secret word so strangers cannot lie.

what multicast address does rip v2 use

tldr.problem: RIP-1 route entries carry no subnet mask, next hop or authentication, so routers had to guess subnet boundaries and trust anyone who sent an update.
tldr.mechanism: RIP-2 reuses the 20-octet route entry and fills the unused fields with a subnet mask, route tag and next hop, sends updates to multicast 224.0.0.9, and may use the first entry for a plain-text password.
tldr.outcome: Small networks get classless routes and some protection with almost no configuration, while the 15-hop limit and slow convergence keep it out of larger networks.

sections.title: Introduction and Justification
sections.content:
RIP is a routing protocol for the inside of a network. RFC 2453 begins by admitting that, with OSPF and IS-IS available, "there are those who believe that RIP is obsolete". Its answer is that in a small network RIP has very little overhead in bandwidth, configuration and management time, is easy to implement, and has far more implementations in the field than OSPF and IS-IS combined.

So the document does not replace RIP. It increases its usefulness at low cost. Version 1, specified in RFC 1058, was missing three things that later networks needed: subnet masks, a way to say which router to forward to, and authentication. RIP-2 adds them while staying backwards compatible with RIP-1 routers.

RFC 2453 obsoletes RFC 1723, is also published as STD 56, and was updated by RFC 4822, which adds cryptographic authentication.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school where each class monitor tells the next class how many doors away every room is. This is an old, simple way to do it, and this memo teaches it a few new tricks.

sections.title: How Distance-Vector Routing Works
sections.content:
RIP is based on the Bellman-Ford, or distance vector, algorithm. Each router keeps a table with one entry per destination holding the destination address, a metric (the total cost), the next-hop router, a route change flag and timers. The table starts with the directly connected networks, normally at cost 1, so the metric is usually a plain hop count.

Routers send their tables to neighbours. When an update arrives, the receiver adds the cost of the network it came over and adopts the route if the new metric is smaller. If the update comes from the router the current route already uses, the receiver always accepts it, even if the metric got worse. That is how bad news spreads.

Only routers need to speak RIP. A host with one interface has nothing useful to contribute, so non-routers need not send updates at all.

The metric is an integer from 1 to 15. The value 16 means "infinity", that is, unreachable. The 15-hop limit is a deliberate trade-off, explained in the next section.
sections.eli5: Each router keeps a notebook of how far away every place is. When a neighbour says "I am 2 steps from the library," you write down 3, because you are one step from the neighbour. If a number would reach 16, it means "you cannot get there."

sections.title: Preventing Loops and Instability
sections.content:
The basic algorithm always converges, but it can take a long time when a network disappears. Routers can keep passing a dead route back and forth, raising the metric each time, until it reaches 16. The RFC calls this "counting to infinity" and chooses infinity as small as possible so the counting stops quickly. This is why RIP is limited to networks whose longest path is 15 hops.

Split horizon
Never advertise a route back to the neighbour it was learned from. This is simple split horizon.
Poisoned reverse
Advertise it back, but with metric 16, which breaks two-router loops at once. It makes updates larger, so implementations may choose simple split horizon.
Triggered updates
When a metric changes, send an update almost immediately instead of waiting for the 30-second timer.
Rate limit
After a triggered update, wait a random 1 to 5 seconds before sending another, and include at least the changed routes.

Per RFC 1812, implementations must use split horizon and should also use poisoned reverse. Loops involving three or more routers can still happen, which is why the hop limit remains the final safeguard.
sections.eli5: If you told your friend "the shortest way to the park is through you," and then they told you the same thing back, you would both be wrong forever. So you never tell someone about a path you learned from them, or you shout "that way is closed!" instead.

sections.title: Message Format
sections.content:
RIP runs over UDP. Every router sends and receives on port 520. Unsolicited updates use 520 as both source and destination port. A reply to a specific request goes back to the requester's source port, and one-off queries may come from any port as long as they target 520.

A message starts with a 4-octet header: a command (1 for request, 2 for response), a version (1 or 2) and two octets that must be zero. After it come 1 to 25 route entries of 20 octets each. In RIP-2 an entry holds the address family identifier, a route tag, the IPv4 address, the subnet mask, the next hop and the metric. The route tag, subnet mask and next hop sit in positions that RIP-1 defined as must-be-zero fields, which is why the new version can coexist with the old.

If the first entry has address family 0xFFFF it is an authentication entry rather than a route, which leaves at most 24 route entries in that message.
sections.eli5: A RIP message is a short note with a header and a list of lines. Each line says "this place, this big, go through that door, it costs this much."

sections.title: What RIP-2 Adds
sections.content:
Section 4 turns the previously unused fields into features.

Subnet mask
Applied to the IP address to give the non-host portion. A zero mask means none was included. This removes RIP-1's guesswork about subnets versus hosts.
Route tag
An attribute that must be preserved and readvertised, intended to separate internal RIP routes from external ones imported from an EGP or another IGP.
Next hop
The router to which packets should be forwarded. 0.0.0.0 means the sender itself. It is advisory and must be directly reachable on the subnet.
Multicast
Periodic updates go to 224.0.0.9 so hosts that do not care about RIP can ignore them. IGMP is not needed because these messages are never forwarded.

The next-hop field helps when only some routers on a segment run RIP-2. Appendix A shows a campus whose internal routers learn routes from just one external router, which names the correct exit for each network, so no packet takes an extra hop.
sections.eli5: Version 2 adds four labels to each line: how big the neighbourhood is, a sticker saying where the news came from, a hint about a quicker door, and a way to whisper to only the routers instead of shouting to everyone.

sections.title: Timers, Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Every 30 seconds a router sends its whole table as an unsolicited response to its neighbours. To prevent routers synchronizing and colliding, the timer must either run from a clock unaffected by load or be offset by a random 0 to 5 seconds each time.

Each route has a timeout and a garbage-collection timer. If 180 seconds pass without an update for a route, it expires. Its metric is set to 16, the change flag is set, a triggered update is signalled and a 120-second garbage-collection timer starts. The route stays in updates as unreachable until that timer expires, so neighbours hear it is gone.

A router that has just started multicasts a request. A request with exactly one entry, address family 0 and metric 16, asks for the whole table, and the answer gets normal split horizon. A request listing specific destinations is answered as is, with no split horizon, since it is expected to be diagnostic.

On receiving a response, a router ignores it if it is not from port 520, is not from a directly connected neighbour, or is its own output. Each entry is checked for a valid destination and a metric from 1 to 16, then the metric becomes MIN(metric + cost, 16).
sections.eli5: Routers chat every 30 seconds. If a neighbour goes quiet for three minutes, you decide its roads are closed, and keep saying so for two more minutes so everyone hears.

sections.title: Compatibility with RIP-1
sections.content:
RFC 1058 said version 0 messages are discarded, version 1 messages are discarded if a must-be-zero field is non-zero, and messages with a higher version are not discarded merely for non-zero must-be-zero fields. A RIP-1 router therefore reads a RIP-2 message and ignores the extras.

Because some RIP-1 implementations do not follow that rule, and multicast would hide RIP-2 updates from RIP-1 routers, a per-interface compatibility switch is required. Its sending settings are RIP-1, RIP-1 compatibility (RIP-2 messages broadcast), RIP-2 (multicast) and none. The recommended default is RIP-1 or RIP-2, not RIP-1 compatibility. A matching receive control accepts RIP-1 only, RIP-2 only, both, or none.

On networks mixing both versions the semantics should stay at RIP-1 level: use a single subnet mask and disable auto-summarization. The RFC also declines to raise infinity above 16, since older routers would simply ignore such routes.
sections.eli5: Old routers and new routers can share the same wire. New ones can talk quietly in the old way, loudly to everyone, or privately to just the new routers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that "the basic RIP protocol is not a secure protocol." To improve on that, RIP-2 defines authentication in the first route entry. The only type defined here is type 2, a simple password: the remaining 16 octets hold a plain text password, left-justified and padded with nulls.

The acceptance rules are strict. A router not configured to authenticate accepts RIP-1 and unauthenticated RIP-2, and discards authenticated RIP-2. A router configured to authenticate accepts RIP-1 and RIP-2 that pass the check, and discards unauthenticated or failed messages. For maximum security RIP-1 should be ignored when authentication is on, or its unauthenticated copies of the information will propagate.

A plain text password is sent in every message, so anyone who can see the traffic can read and replay it. The RFC points to RFC 2082 for stronger MD5 authentication, which RFC 4822 later replaced. Authentication also does not hide RIP-2 messages from RIP-1 routers, which skip the 0xFFFF entry.
sections.eli5: The secret word in version 2 is written on every note in plain letters. It stops people who do not know it from joining, but anyone who watches the notes go by can learn it. Later rules added a proper lock.

today: RIP-2 is still found on small office and lab networks, in simple embedded and home routers, and as a built-in option in router operating systems and routing daemons. Larger networks generally use OSPF, IS-IS or BGP. For IPv6 the equivalent is RIPng (RFC 2080). The MD5 authentication of RFC 2082 was later obsoleted by RFC 4822.
